items.title: Expose your design system to LLMs
items.summary: Hardik Pandya (Atlassian) lays out a concrete method to stop AI coding tools from inventing colours, spacings, and components: write plain-Markdown spec files for the system's rules, expose a named token layer the model can quote from, and add automated audits that fail builds when a generated screen drifts off-system.
items.why: This is the primary source behind the Smashing piece you flagged earlier this week — the actual playbook, not someone's summary of it. Directly mappable onto CueDesign: spec files for your tokens and rules so generated screens inherit them rather than guess.

items.title: Reviewing code in the agent era
items.summary: Linear's design engineer on what changes when AI agents are writing half your team's pull requests: the reviewer stops chasing line-by-line correctness and instead judges whether the change fits the product's system and actually solves the problem.
items.why: Same shift is coming for design review at Cuemath as your team uses AI to generate screens. The frame here — review the fit and the judgment, not the pixels — is the exact muscle to teach designers as agent output volume goes up.

items.title: TBM 426: The Trouble With Mirrors
items.summary: Cutler argues that org transparency efforts often misfire because people want to feel heard (mirroring) before they can absorb uncomfortable truths (mirrors). The fix isn't more dashboards — it's collaborative sense-making before clarity is imposed.
items.why: Useful framing for how you roll out design-system audits, learning data, or process changes inside Cuemath: lead with shared exploration, not a verdict. Saves you from a transparency push that lands as judgment.

items.title: Phonopolis: an entire game crafted from cardboard and paper
items.summary: Amanita Design's new puzzle adventure was built almost entirely as physical cardboard-and-paper sets — handcrafted, sandpapered, photographed, then converted into the game's 3D world. The dystopia-by-craft aesthetic is unlike anything currently shipping.
items.why: Amanita is the rare game studio whose visual world feels handmade in a way kids' learning products almost never attempt. A concrete reference for pushing MathGym's art direction toward texture and character instead of the default rounded-vector look.

items.title: The View From Cairo: minimalism, power, and Arab design critique
items.summary: Cairo-based designer Moe Elhossieny argues that the global default of clean Western minimalism is being exported into Arab branding (case study: the Grand Egyptian Museum) and is crowding out local visual languages — partly because the region has too little public design criticism to push back.
items.why: Sharp prompt for Cuemath's brand and product look in Indian and MENA markets: where are you reaching for the default international-startup minimalism vs. drawing on local visual culture that would actually feel like home to your kids and parents?
